$comment: Artists and artworks behind the artist shops. Stable ids are the relationship keys: print-catalog prints reference an artwork id (museum) or their collection an artist id (studio). Museum artworks are written by `npm run museum -- fetch`; rights and master reviews are recorded by people with `npm run museum -- review`. Types and validation: app/lib/artRegistry.ts. Brief: docs/artist-shops/brief.md.

artists.name: Katsushika Hokusai
artists.bio: Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849) was a Japanese painter and printmaker of the Edo period who worked in the ukiyo-e tradition for some seven decades. His woodblock series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (c. 1830–32), which includes Under the Wave off Kanagawa, made landscape a central subject of Japanese prints.
artists.curatorNote: We start with Hokusai's landscapes because they hold a room the way they hold the sheet: a decisive line, a few flat colours and a great deal of air. Prints and framed prints keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on a white border; cards, postcards, canvas and phone cases use a chosen detail.

artists.name: Utagawa Hiroshige
artists.bio: Utagawa Hiroshige (1797–1858) was a Japanese ukiyo-e printmaker of the Edo period, known above all for landscape series such as The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō and One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, the last of which he worked on until his death.
artists.curatorNote: Hiroshige's views are quieter than Hokusai's: weather, distance and the small figures who move through them. Prints and framed prints keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on a white border; cards, postcards, canvas and phone cases use a chosen detail.

artists.name: Vasily Kandinsky
artists.bio: Vasily Kandinsky (1866–1944) was a Russian-born painter and theorist who studied law in Moscow before moving to Munich in 1896 to train as an artist. There he co-founded the Blaue Reiter group in 1911, and by 1913 he was painting pictures with no recognisable subject; his book On the Spiritual in Art (1911) argued that colour and form could act on the viewer as directly as music. He later taught at the Bauhaus and spent his last years in France.
artists.curatorNote: These five paintings come from 1909 to 1913, the Murnau and Munich years in which Kandinsky's landscapes loosened into colour and line until the subject could hardly be read. Hanger, acrylic and metal prints, cushions and blankets keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on white.

artists.name: Piet Mondrian
artists.bio: Piet Mondrian (1872–1944) was a Dutch painter who began with landscapes and flower studies in the tradition of the Hague School, worked through Cubism in Paris from 1912, and arrived at a strict abstraction of black lines, white grounds and the three primary colours. In 1917 he was a founder of the De Stijl group with Theo van Doesburg, and he called his approach Neo-Plasticism. He lived in Paris and London before moving to New York in 1940, where he died in 1944.
artists.curatorNote: We show Mondrian's route as well as where it led: a Dutch field and a single chrysanthemum beside the 1921 lozenge and the grids of 1927 and 1935. Hanger, acrylic and metal prints, cushions and blankets keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on white.

artists.name: Clara Mendes Studio
artists.bio: Studio works are made with generative image tools from Clara Mendes briefs, then selected and prepared for print by the studio. They are labelled as generated wherever they appear.

artists.name: Vincent van Gogh
artists.bio: Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890) was a Dutch painter who worked as an art dealer, a teacher and a lay preacher before he turned to art around 1880. After years of dark peasant scenes in the Netherlands he moved to Paris in 1886, where his colour brightened, and in 1888 to Arles in the south of France. He spent his last year at the asylum in Saint-Rémy and in Auvers-sur-Oise, where he died in 1890, having made most of his paintings in the last decade of his life.
artists.curatorNote: Three paintings from his last two years in the south of France: the asylum garden at Saint-Rémy, a wheat field under a cypress, and the café in Arles he painted by night. Throw blankets, cushions and mugs keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on a plain off-white mount.

artists.name: Claude Monet
artists.bio: Claude Monet (1840–1926) was a French painter and a founder of Impressionism; his Impression, Sunrise, shown in 1874, gave the movement its name. From the 1890s he painted the same subject again and again in changing light, in series of wheatstacks, poplars and the façade of Rouen Cathedral. From 1883 he lived at Giverny, where he made the garden and water-lily pond that he painted for the last three decades of his life.
artists.curatorNote: Two of Monet’s long looks at one subject: wheatstacks on a winter morning from the 1891 series, and the water-lily pond at Giverny that occupied his last years. Throw blankets, cushions and mugs keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on a plain off-white mount.

artists.name: Gustav Klimt
artists.bio: Gustav Klimt (1862–1918) was an Austrian painter who trained at the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts and began with decorative commissions for theatres and museums. In 1897 he was a founder and the first president of the Vienna Secession. His portraits and allegories, some laid with gold leaf, combine flat ornament with closely painted faces and hands.
artists.curatorNote: Klimt painted Mäda Primavesi, the nine-year-old daughter of a banker and patron of the Wiener Werkstätte, standing square to the viewer against a field of flowers. Throw blankets, cushions and mugs keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on a plain off-white mount.

artists.name: Johannes Vermeer
artists.bio: Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) was a Dutch painter who spent his life in Delft, where he joined the painters’ guild in 1653. Fewer than forty paintings are attributed to him. Most show one or two figures in a quiet interior lit from a window at the left, painted slowly and with costly pigments such as natural ultramarine.
artists.curatorNote: The Milkmaid is one of Vermeer’s few scenes of work: a kitchen maid pouring milk by the window, with bread on the table and the wall behind her left almost bare. Throw blankets, cushions and mugs keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on a plain off-white mount.

artists.name: William Morris
artists.bio: William Morris (1834–1896) was an English designer, writer and socialist and a leading figure of the Arts and Crafts movement. In 1861 he co-founded the decorating firm that became Morris & Co., which made wallpapers, printed and woven textiles, furniture and stained glass. Many of his patterns draw on the plants and birds of the English countryside; in 1891 he founded the Kelmscott Press.
artists.curatorNote: Strawberry Thief, designed in 1883, shows the thrushes that took strawberries from Morris’s kitchen garden at Kelmscott Manor; this length of the printed cotton was made by Morris & Co. Throw blankets, cushions and mugs keep the full composition of the printed pattern as the museum photographed it, without the cloth’s plain borders, set on a plain off-white mount.

artists.name: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
artists.bio: Pierre-Auguste Renoir (1841–1919) was a French painter who trained as a painter of porcelain before studying art in Paris, where he met Monet, Sisley and Bazille. He showed at the first Impressionist exhibitions and became known for scenes of Parisian leisure, portraits and nudes. In his last years he lived at Cagnes-sur-Mer and kept painting despite severe arthritis.
artists.curatorNote: Renoir painted flowers throughout his life; these roses from about 1890 are loosely brushed in warm reds and creams. Throw blankets, cushions and mugs keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on a plain off-white mount.

artists.name: Edgar Degas
artists.bio: Edgar Degas (1834–1917) was a French painter, printmaker and sculptor who trained in the classical tradition and admired Ingres. He showed at most of the Impressionist exhibitions, though he called himself a realist, and he worked in oil, pastel and monotype as well as wax. Dancers of the Paris Opéra, at rehearsal more often than on stage, were his most frequent subject.
artists.curatorNote: The Dance Class (1874) shows a rehearsal at the Paris Opéra, with the ballet master Jules Perrot leaning on his stick while the dancers wait their turn. Throw blankets, cushions and mugs keep the full composition as the museum photographed it, set on a plain off-white mount.
